1.title: The Scrum Team and the Developers
1.text: Welcome to Module 3: The Scrum Team and the Developers. So far you have seen the theory and the values. Now we meet the people. You will learn what a Scrum Team is, why it has no sub-teams, what the Developers are accountable for, and how the three accountabilities work together in a Sprint.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Describe the Scrum Team: its members, its size and its focus. Explain what cross-functional and self-managing mean. Give benefits of such a team. State what the Developers are accountable for. Show how the three accountabilities interact in a Sprint. And spot the traps: sub-teams, assigned work, and answers that say only one party is accountable.

1.title: Case Check-In: A Separate Data Team?
1.text: At RideLoop, the Architecture Group has an idea. Create a separate data team for the analytics pipeline, and let the Developers hand that work over. Sofia, the data engineer, is the only person who knows the pipeline today, so the idea sounds tempting. As Scrum Master, you ask a different question: should the Scrum Team share that skill, or hand the work to someone else? The next slides give you the answer.

1.title: The Scrum Team at a Glance
1.text: The Scrum Team is one team with three accountabilities: a Scrum Master, a Product Owner, and Developers. Inside it there are no sub-teams and no hierarchy. The team focuses on the Product Goal, one objective at a time. It is typically ten or fewer people. If it grows beyond that, it becomes several Scrum Teams that share one Product Goal, one Product Backlog and one Product Owner. In the earlier edition you will find a Development Team of three to nine, called self-organizing. A sub-team, a team lead or a manager who assigns work contradicts the Guide.

1.title: Cross-Functional and Self-Managing
1.text: Two words define how the team works. Cross-functional means that together the members have every skill needed to create value each Sprint. It does not mean everybody does everything. The diagram shows it: no single person covers all the skills, but the team does. Self-managing means the members decide who does what, when and how. It does not mean no rules, and it does not mean no Product Owner. The team works within the framework, toward the Product Goal. That settles the RideLoop question: the team shares the skill, with Sofia pairing with Tomas and Wei, instead of handing the pipeline to a separate team.

1.title: Responsible, Accountable, Empowered
1.text: Three more facts about the team. It is responsible for all product activities: working with stakeholders, verification, maintenance, operation, experiments, research and development, and anything else required. As a whole, it is accountable for "creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint." The organization structures and empowers it to manage its own work, and if managers override the team, the Scrum Master helps them understand. And a sustainable pace improves its focus and consistency. If an option says only the Developers, or only the Product Owner, is accountable for the Increment, it is wrong.

1.title: Benefits of This Kind of Team
1.text: Why build teams this way? The Guide states the design; the usual benefits go beyond it, so this slide carries the tag Beyond the Guide. Fewer hand-offs, because everything needed is inside the team. Faster decisions and adaptation, because whoever learns something can decide at once. Higher quality, through shared ownership. Motivation and ownership, because people choose how to do the work. Skill sharing, so knowledge spreads. And better collaboration: one team, one goal, one Product Backlog. Name at least three.

1.title: The Developers
1.text: Now the Developers. They are the people on the Scrum Team who build the usable Increment, whatever part they work on, every Sprint. The skills needed are broad, and depend on the domain of work. The word is inclusive: testers, designers, analysts and other specialists who build the Increment are Developers. At RideLoop there are seven Developers, and that includes Lena, the quality engineer, and Jonas, the designer. A person does not need the job title developer.

1.title: What the Developers Are Always Accountable For
1.text: The Developers are always accountable for four things. First, the Sprint Backlog: they select the work and plan how to do it. Second, quality: they follow a Definition of Done, and unfinished work is not part of the Increment. Third, daily adaptation: they adapt the plan each day toward the Sprint Goal. Fourth, mutual accountability: they hold each other to professional standards. The Developers own the how and the Sprint plan. They do not own the order of the Product Backlog.

1.title: Other Developer Duties in the Guide
1.text: The Guide gives the Developers more duties, spread across the framework. In Sprint Planning they select items, in discussion with the Product Owner, and plan the work. They size Product Backlog items, because the people who will do the work are best placed to judge it. They run the Daily Scrum and choose its structure. When work turns out different from expected, they negotiate scope with the Product Owner, without harming the Sprint Goal. And they meet the Definition of Done.

1.title: Who Is Accountable for What
1.text: Think of accountability in layers. The outer layer is the entire Scrum Team: it holds the Increment, all the product activities, and the events. Inside it, the Developers hold the Sprint plan, quality and the daily plan. The Product Owner holds the value of the product and the Product Backlog. The Scrum Master holds the establishing of Scrum and the effectiveness of the team. Each one adds a part, and the whole team stands behind the result.

1.title: How the Three Work Together in a Sprint
1.text: How do the three work together? In Sprint Planning, the Product Owner proposes value, the Developers select and plan, and the Scrum Master ensures the event works. During the Sprint, the Product Owner refines the Product Backlog, which means adding detail to items. The Developers build and adapt their plan daily, and the Scrum Master coaches and helps remove impediments. At the Sprint Review, the Scrum Team shows its results to key stakeholders, and they discuss progress toward the Product Goal. At the Retrospective, all three take part as members of the team.

1.title: Scrum Team or Work Group?
1.text: Compare a Scrum Team with a traditional work group. This comparison goes beyond the Guide, but it explains the exam logic. A Scrum Team is one team with no hierarchy, and it decides who does what. Its skills are held collectively, and the entire team is accountable for the Increment. A traditional group has departments with managers, who assign tasks and hand work from one specialist group to the next. When an option sounds like the right-hand column, it contradicts Scrum.

1.title: Traps: What the Exam Expects
1.text: Here are the traps. No sub-teams and no hierarchies: a test team, a design team or a team lead inside the Scrum Team is wrong. Typically ten or fewer, because small teams talk to each other more easily and get more done; a larger group becomes several Scrum Teams. Cross-functional is collective, not everyone doing everything. Self-managing means nobody outside assigns the tasks. The whole Scrum Team is accountable for the Increment. And watch the old wording: Development Team, self-organizing, and three to nine members. The Developers decide how, and nobody else tells them.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. The Scrum Team is one team: a Scrum Master, a Product Owner and Developers. It is typically ten or fewer people. It is cross-functional and self-managing: all the skills, and its own decisions. The whole team answers for the Increment. The Developers are accountable for the Sprint plan, quality, daily adaptation and mutual accountability. And together they work toward one Product Goal. Now test yourself.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Jonas Berg, the RideLoop UX designer, says that designers are not developers, so the Daily Scrum is not for Jonas. What is the best reply? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. A Developer is anyone on the Scrum Team who builds some part of the usable Increment, and the word covers everyone who does the work. A designer who helps create the Increment is a Developer.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. The RideLoop Developers ask Maya to assign each of them a share of the Sprint Backlog items. What should the Scrum Master do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. A self-managing Scrum Team decides internally who does what, when and how, and the Scrum Master coaches it in self-management. Assignment by the Product Owner, the Scrum Master or a manager takes that away.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. After a Sprint in which the Increment did not meet the Definition of Done, Grace asks who is accountable. What is the best answer? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. The whole Scrum Team answers for the Increment each Sprint. The Developers follow the Definition of Done, but the whole team stands behind the Increment.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which set lists what the Developers are always accountable for? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C: the Sprint plan, quality through the Definition of Done, daily adaptation, and holding each other accountable. The other sets belong to the Product Owner and the Scrum Master.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which is a benefit of a cross-functional, self-managing Scrum Team? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. With all the skills inside the team, there are fewer hand-offs and delays, and the team adapts the moment it learns something. It still has a Product Owner, a Definition of Done and stakeholders.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: C. Developers means everyone who helps create the Increment. Question two: A. A self-managing team decides who does what. Question three: D. The whole Scrum Team answers for the Increment. Question four: C. Sprint plan, quality, daily adaptation, mutual accountability. Question five: B. Fewer hand-offs. That completes Module 3. Next, Module 4 covers the Product Owner.
